source.title: Eliciting Weak-to-Strong Generalization with On-Policy Reverse Distillation
source.authors: Youngrok Park; Sangmin Bae; Hojung Jung; Jongwoo Ko; Yunseon Choi; Young Jin Kim; Pashmina Cameron; Aaron C. Courville; SeYoung Yun

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present through Appendix L.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether a stronger student can benefit from weaker-model guidance and outperform its supervisor, but uses verifier-driven RL with gradient scaling rather than fine-tuning on weak labels, and does not calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own OPRD, RL, and distillation results, so these are included. It does not calculate PGR. Results from cited papers are not included. The paper also reports style comparisons, guidance-direction and scaling ablations, teacher-checkpoint comparisons, and reference-policy/gradient-signal challenges; relevant separately reported results are recorded below.
record.test_reason: Only the teacher-only baselines bear on the claim: OPD, MOPD, Direct-OPD and W2S-OPD. These are the study's own runs, and the student learns only from the weaker model's signal, with no gold reward. They give a different-method (on-policy distillation) test of whether a larger student beats its weak supervisor (V1, V6) and whether a weak-only training change helps over plain OPD (V2). OPRD, GRPO, KDRL, Mix-RL and S2L-PO all train on the gold verifier reward. A student exceeding the teacher there is not weak-to-strong generalization: GRPO with no teacher at all also exceeds the teacher on math (39.38 vs 38.66). So the study's headline OPRD results do not test any version. No PGR is computed, and no strong ceiling trained on gold labels is defined.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that OPRD, which rescales the student's verifier-driven gradient along the weak teacher's post-training shift, reaches teacher-level performance in fewer updates and keeps improving beyond the teacher, whereas OPD plateaus near the teacher. They report that the gains also hold strong-to-weak, and they note vanishing-gradient and length-bias limitations. The paraphrase should add that the gains depend on the gold verifier reward.
record.recipe_differences: Uses verifier-driven RL and on-policy gradient scaling guided by the weak teacher's post-training policy shift, rather than fine-tuning on weak labels; no PGR calculation.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with amplification strength, teacher checkpoint quality, the construction of the guidance direction, the alignment-branch schedule, the teacher reference checkpoint, and whether verifier-driven student gradients are nonzero. The paper reports that reference choice can affect length bias and task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: When the student also trains on gold verifier reward, OPRD exceeds the weak teacher and every baseline in math, Reasoning Gym, code, visual tool use and multi-teacher consolidation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Using a weaker teacher's post-training shift to rescale verifier-driven RL gradients speeds up RL and lets the student pass the teacher. This is RL acceleration with gold reward, not weak-to-strong generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: In strong-to-weak transfer, OPRD beats OPD, GRPO and KDRL but stays below the stronger teacher on checkpoint averages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verifier-guided teacher-shift scaling also helps when the teacher is larger than the student.

fits_no_version.finding: The choice of teacher reference checkpoint can inject a length bias into the guidance signal; a later reference fixes it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OPRD outcomes depend on the reference checkpoint when the teacher's shift includes reward-irrelevant length changes.

fits_no_version.finding: OPRD cannot help when verifier gradients vanish; OPD (40.5%) outperforms it in that regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: OPRD's correction requires nonzero verifier gradients.

fits_no_version.finding: OPD's response style moves toward the teacher over training, while OPRD stays closer to the GRPO student.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher-shift scaling transfers guidance without the student imitating the teacher's style.

record.problems: No PGR is calculated, and the method differs from fine-tuning on weak labels because it relies on verifier-driven RL. The paper reports evaluation-time response-resampling uncertainty for math and reasoning, but says multi-seed post-training is prohibitively expensive. Several learning-curve and ablation results are presented as figures rather than exact numerical values. The paper itself notes that its logit-space stationarity result does not establish preservation of stationary points in neural-network parameter space.
record.rows_left_out: The main tables report individual benchmark scores in addition to the recorded reported aggregates; these were omitted where an aggregate was explicitly reported. Other appendix results include Qwen3-Base math and additional Reasoning Gym tasks (Table 9, Figures 12–13), detailed per-task and training-curve results (Figures 8–18), branch-only and branch-scheduling ablations (Figures 6–7), guidance-direction comparisons (Figures 3a and 18), and computational cost and memory measurements (Tables 11–12). These were not individually extracted because they exceed the concise set of rows needed to represent each tested version and the main reported outcome; no PGR values are supplied for them.

untested.parts: No PGR and no strong ceiling trained on gold labels. Only on-policy distillation variants are run, not fine-tuning on weak labels.
No auxiliary confidence loss, supervisor ensembling or loss variants. The only weak-only method contrast is W2S-OPD and Direct-OPD vs OPD, run on three tasks.
No weak-only sweep over supervisor or student size. The teacher-quality ablation is run only under verifier-reward OPRD. Nothing on what predicts PGR.
Not tested. The stationarity result concerns verifier-reward OPRD, not weak-only supervision.
Only agentic visual tool use with Qwen2.5-VL, and only with OPD as the weak-only method. No image-classification setting.

missing.what: Per-task weak-only results against the teacher: OPD 46.92/55.00/35.10 vs teacher 42.50/57.50/32.00; Direct-OPD 35.04/49.20/29.20; W2S-OPD 52.96/59.50/35.20; OPD average 45.67. Columns are AIME'24, Knights & Knaves, String Manipulation.
Text says W2S-OPD passes the weak teacher but plateaus near teacher level.
W2SR-P (SFT on teacher trajectories filtered by the gold verifier) averages 48.64 vs teacher 44.00. Gold filtering makes it only partly weak supervision.
Qwen3-Base OPD results: math average 20.48 vs teacher 20.50; three extra Reasoning Gym tasks average 46.50 vs 44.00 (Zebra 29.10 vs 31.00, Color Cube 48.30 vs 46.00, Binary Matrix 62.10 vs 55.00).
Per-family OPD agent scores vs teacher: Maze 81.48 vs 85.94, GPT4Scene 64.74 vs 64.67, SR-91k 47.02 vs 50.38, Spatial VQA 69.04 vs 69.99.
Statement that OPD plateaus near the teacher average, and per-benchmark OPD curves.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all OPRD, GRPO and KDRL rows to V1–V3. Those methods train on ground-truth verifier reward, so beating the teacher there says nothing about learning from weak supervision; GRPO alone beats the teacher in math. I relinked only the teacher-only methods (OPD, MOPD, Direct-OPD, W2S-OPD) to V1, V2 and V6. Their results show little or no gain over the teacher, except W2S-OPD. All trained-policy values are five-checkpoint averages that include early checkpoints, which biases them downward relative to final performance. There is no strong ceiling, so PGR cannot be computed. Seeds are single; only response-resampling standard deviations are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ordinary fine-tuning on weak labels or calculate PGR; OPRD also uses verifier-driven RL.
Compares OPRD and other training methods by task scores, not PGR. Does not test auxiliary confidence losses or ensembling weak supervisors.
Varies model sizes, tasks, and settings, but does not establish which representations predict PGR or report PGR.
Does not test distribution shift, students exploiting what supervisors cannot check, or whether gains shrink when teacher and student errors overlap.
Does not establish conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor. Its optimization argument concerns stationary points and an ascent bound for a fixed-response logit-space objective.
Tests agentic visual tool use with Qwen2.5-VL; does not test other vision settings or calculate PGR.

relationships.condition: Plain on-policy distillation from a smaller GRPO-trained Qwen3 teacher (math, Reasoning Gym, code, multi-teacher)
